b:
With today's rise of agentic AI, well-discoverable and processable
business data has become the cornerstone of any company's journey towards
a data-driven business. In large companies, this valuable data is created
at various places within the company, with different teams being most
knowledgeable about a particular topic. Therefore, creating valuable
analytics or data applications is usually about pulling data together from
various sources to connect them meaningfully. In this process of
combining data from many sources, trust in the data becomes a major
factor.

Imagine Alex, a data engineer at a multinational insurance company,
building a customer insights application that predicts the likelihood of
customers buying additional insurance products. In the company's data
warehouse, Alex found a dataset that seems to contain most of the
information needed to make this prediction, but Alex has several
questions:
Does the dataset have all the information I need and in what form?

Does the data contain the information and have the meaning that I think it
does?
Is it connected to other datasets? If so, which?
How fresh and complete is the data, and of what quality?

Can I rely on its structure remaining stable so my application won't break
in the future?
Am I allowed to process the data for my purpose, for example under the GDPR?

Do I have to apply special precautions, for example for personal data, when
processing the data or resharing the results?
With whom may I share the resulting predictions?

The questions above can be categorized in various ways, but they show
that the matter of trust is not only about whether Alex can trust the source
of the data (in terms of quality, reliability, legal issues) but also
whether the recipients of the results are trustworthy to take care of the
data.

Data contracts are a way to answer these questions not just once, but to
ensure the trustworthy processing of data continuously.

In its simplest form, a data contract is a description of the
shape of the data that a data provider is offering, e.g., a schema. Here
is an excerpt of what the description of the dataset that Alex found
could look like. We will illustrate all the examples using the Open Data
Contract Standard (ODCS) as it is the de facto industry standard
governed by the Bitol project at the Linux Foundation (rated Adopt in the Thoughtworks
Technology Radar).

apiVersion: "v3.2.0"
kind: "DataContract"
id: "customers"
name: "Customers"
version: "1.0.0"
status: "active"

schema:
  - name: "customers"
    physicalType: "TABLE"
    description: "All customers holding a life insurance policy since 2020-01-01"
    properties:
      - name: "customer_id"
        logicalType: "string"
        primaryKey: true
      - name: "customer_name"
        businessName: "Customer Name"
        logicalType: "string"
        physicalType: "VARCHAR(100)"
        examples:
          - "Alex Doe"
        classification: "restricted"

Seeing this simple data contract, most likely rendered as a page in
the company's data marketplace rather than as raw YAML, Alex already has
a much better idea
whether the data will be sufficient for implementing the prediction. But
Alex is wondering when the data was last updated and if the declared
fields will consistently contain correct data. In ODCS, there are specific
elements to describe the quality of the data through quality rules as well
as service levels that specify runtime behavior over time. Here is how the
data contract can be extended to address these issues:

schema:
  - name: "customers"
    properties:
      - name: "customer_name"
        quality:
          - type: "sql"
            description: "Expect less than 1% empty name fields"
            query: |
              SELECT AVG(
                CASE
                  WHEN customer_name IS NULL
                    OR TRIM(customer_name) = ''
                  THEN 1
                  ELSE 0
                END
              )
              FROM customers
            mustBeLessThan: 0.01
slaProperties:
  - property: "freshness"
    value: 24
    unit: "hours"
    element: "customers.last_updated_at"
    description: "Within 24 hours of the last update"

Seeing these guarantees, Alex has much more confidence that building an
application based on this dataset will be sustainable and not fall apart
at the next update of the dataset: the active status and the 1.0.0
version indicate that this is a stable and maintained dataset; the
quality and SLA descriptions allow for processing the data reliably. And
actual trust comes when these guarantees are verified automatically.
What Does This Mean for AI Agents?

Now imagine that Alex is not a human but an AI agent. A human who
distrusts data hesitates, or asks the people who own it. An agent does
neither: as Pramod Sadalage and Prem Chandrasekaran put it in Making
Your Data Ready for Agentic AI, agents treat every value as truth.
Where a lack of trust slows humans down, it makes agents produce
confidently wrong results, and humans in turn stop trusting agents to
work with data on their own. Data contracts break that loop by giving
agents the explicit metadata they would otherwise have to guess.

An agent has the same questions Alex had, on every task, and nobody
to ask. A data contract answers them in a form the agent can act on:
published to a marketplace that agents can search, it makes the data
discoverable in the first place; its schema and semantics tell the
agent how to query and join the data correctly; its quality rules and
service levels tell it how far to trust the result; and its terms of
use tell it what it is allowed to do. That is why agentic use cases,
from chatting with your data to generating whole data pipelines, are
becoming one of the main reasons to adopt data contracts.

Before we look at the individual sections, it helps to understand
what characterizes a data contract in the first place. A data contract
is:

Machine-readable. A data contract is a structured document, typically
YAML, not prose buried in a wiki. Tools, pipelines, and AI agents can parse it
and act on it directly, without a human having to translate it first.

Verifiable. Its promises are concrete enough to be checked against
the actual data. A quality rule such as “less than 1% empty names” is not an
aspiration but an assertion that tooling can evaluate and either pass or fail.

Versioned. A data contract carries a version and evolves under a
clear scheme, so consumers can tell a harmless change from a breaking one,
and providers can phase new versions in and old ones out gracefully.

Provider-driven. It is published one-sidedly by the party that
produces the data and knows it best. They own the promises they make, which
shifts responsibility for the interface to where the knowledge sits and where
the promises can be kept or broken.

Consumer-oriented. Even though the provider writes it, it is written
for the consumer: it captures the schema, semantics, quality guarantees, and
terms of use a consumer needs to decide whether the data fits their purpose and
to rely on it over time.

The source of truth for metadata. It is the authoritative description
of the dataset. Catalogs, marketplaces, documentation, and agents all draw from
it, rather than each maintaining their own divergent copy.

Such a data contract is typically defined using the Open Data
Contract Standard.

The Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS) defines a YAML format for
specifying data contracts in a standardized way. You've already seen a
short example of that YAML in the introduction of this article. The
Open Data Contract Standard is part of the Bitol project, a graduate
project of the Linux Foundation, and thereby part of a family of metadata standards.
The specification of the Open Data Contract Standard is publicly
available on GitHub, where it has over 1000 stars. The standard comes with a JSON schema to help
validate YAML files in terms of standard compliance.
Figure 1: The sections of the Open Data Contract Standard v3.2

The Open Data Contract Standard comprises many different
categories of metadata, which we will cover shortly using example code
snippets for each part based on ODCS 3.2, the latest version at the
time of writing. An interactive,
step-by-step walkthrough of the same sections is available on
datacontract.com.

apiVersion: "v3.2.0"
kind: "DataContract"
id: "customers"
name: "Customers"
version: "1.0.0"
status: "active"

Every data contract starts with its fundamentals: the version of
the standard, unique identifier, name, data contract version number,
and status. This metadata identifies the contract and enables
versioning as well as lifecycle.

schema:
  - name: "customers"
    physicalType: "TABLE"
    description: "All customers holding a life insurance policy since 2020-01-01"
    properties:
      - name: "customer_id"
        logicalType: "string"
        primaryKey: true
      - name: "customer_name"
        businessName: "Customer Name"
        logicalType: "string"
        physicalType: "VARCHAR(100)"
        required: true
        examples:
          - "Alex Doe"
        classification: "restricted"
        tags:
          - "pii:true"
      - name: "annual_premium"
        logicalType: "integer"
        physicalType: "INTEGER"
        description: "Annual premium in cents"
        required: true
        logicalTypeOptions:
          minimum: 0
      - name: "customer_status"
        logicalType: "string"
        physicalType: "TEXT"
        examples:
          - "active"
      - name: "last_updated_at"
        logicalType: "date"
        physicalType: "TIMESTAMP"
        description: "Timestamp of the last update to the customer record"

The schema defines the structure and semantics of your data. In
our example that is a table with its columns, but the same structure
describes the messages of a Kafka topic, files in an object store,
or the payload of an API. Each column includes technical details,
business semantics, and governance attributes. For example, that
the annual premium is stored in cents
as an integer, following the company's convention on how to handle
monetary values. You can also define relationships like foreign keys
between columns and tables within the data contract.

schema:
  - name: "customers"
    quality:
      - type: "sql"
        description: "Expect more than 100K rows"
        query: "select count(*) from customers"
        mustBeGreaterThan: 100000
    properties:
      - name: "customer_name"
        quality:
          - type: "sql"
            description: "Expect less than 1% empty name fields"
            query: |
              SELECT AVG(
                CASE
                  WHEN customer_name IS NULL
                    OR TRIM(customer_name) = ''
                  THEN 1
                  ELSE 0
                END
              )
              FROM customers
            mustBeLessThan: 0.01
      - name: "customer_status"
        quality:
          - type: "library"
            description: "Only valid customer statuses"
            metric: "invalidValues"
            arguments:
              validValues:
                - "active"
                - "lapsed"
                - "cancelled"
            mustBe: 0

Data quality rules ensure that data meets expectations. You can
define checks like valid value constraints, row count thresholds,
custom SQL validation logic, or even simply a quality rule in
textual form. Thresholds can be absolute, like a minimum row count,
or relative, like at most 1% empty names. Those checks can be
automatically verified with the right tooling.

team:
  name: "customer-data"
  members:
    - username: "carola@example.com"
      name: "Carola Doe"
      role: "Owner"

support:
  - channel: "#customer-data-support"
    tool: "slack"
    url: "https://example.slack.com/archives/C123456789"

Ownership is central to data contracts. The team defines who
owns and maintains the data contract, including its members with
their roles. Add support channels to specify how data consumers
can reach out to the owners. That reachable responsibility is
critical in building trust in data.

description:
  purpose: "Provides customer master data for analytics and reporting"
  usage: "Used by analytics team for customer insights and cross-sell prediction"
  limitations: "Contains only customers with an active policy"
  authoritativeDefinitions:
    - url: "https://example.com/policies/gdpr-compliance"
      type: "businessDefinition"
      description: "GDPR compliance policy for handling customer data"

The terms of use help data consumers understand what they can
and cannot do with the data, establishing clear governance
boundaries. The standard lets you define the purpose, usage
guidelines, and limitations for your data, as well as point to
external policies such as privacy policies or license
agreements.

slaProperties:
  - property: "retention"
    value: 5
    unit: "year"
    description: "Data will be deleted after 5 years"
  - property: "freshness"
    value: 24
    unit: "hours"
    element: "customers.last_updated_at"
    description: "Within 24 hours of the last update"

Service Level Agreements define guarantees such as freshness
of the data, data retention, or latency. Each one is stated so
that it can be measured: the freshness promise above is checked
against last_updated_at every time the contract is
tested, and a breach alerts the owning team.

servers:
  - server: "production"
    type: "snowflake"
    environment: "prod"
    account: "insurance-corp"
    database: "prod_lifeinsurance"
    schema: "dp_customers_v1"

Servers specify where the data actually lives. They include
the connection details to access the data, excluding any
credentials. The standard supports specifying basically any
system that can hold data directly: data platforms and databases
such as Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Oracle, and Postgres,
event streams such as Kafka, Kinesis, or Pub/Sub, files on S3,
or even CSV files on an SFTP server, and many others.
It also provides the fallback to a custom server type if a
system is not supported.

For an event stream, the server entry names the cluster and
the message format, and the schema describes the topic:

servers:
  - server: "production"
    type: "kafka"
    environment: "prod"
    host: "kafka.example.com:9092"
    format: "avro"

schema:
  - name: "customer_events"
    physicalType: "topic"

roles:
  - role: "customers_reader"
    access: "read"
    description: "Read access to all customer data"

Roles describe how consumers get access to the data. Each
role names an IAM role on the data platform, such as a
Snowflake role, and the kind of access it grants. Providers
often define several roles, for example one that includes
personal data and one that doesn't. The contract doesn't
list who holds a role; that is decided per consumer when an
access request is approved, as we'll see in the section on
data marketplaces.

context:
  instructions: >
    Use this data for analytics on life insurance customers.
    Annual premiums are stored in cents; divide by 100 before
    reporting amounts.
  constraints:
    - constraint: >
        Do not use this data to make decisions about individual
        customers, such as pricing a policy or assessing a claim.
  verifiedStatements:
    - question: "How many active customers do we have?"
      answer: |
        SELECT COUNT(*)
        FROM customers
        WHERE customer_status = 'active'

The AI context is guidance written specifically for AI
agents. The instructions act like a system prompt for the
dataset, for example telling an agent that premiums are
stored in cents. The constraints state what an agent must
not do with the data. And the verified statements pair
common business questions with a query the provider has
checked, so an agent can reuse a correct answer instead of
guessing one.

The price can express an internal charge that
reflects the value of the data. In practice, it is
usually left empty or passes on what accessing the data
actually costs on the platform, as in this example: 10
USD per terabyte scanned.

price:
  priceAmount: 10
  priceCurrency: "USD"
  priceUnit: "per TB scanned"

As every company is different, the standard has two built-in
mechanisms to extend it. Custom properties, available on every
level, carry metadata the standard does not know, such as the
legal entity that provides the data, or a reference to a platform
manifest that drives infrastructure provisioning. Vendors use the
same mechanism to add functionality on top. Authoritative
definitions link the contract, or any element in it, to something
defined elsewhere, including other open standards: in the example
below, the OpenAPI specification of a REST API that serves the
same data. Our advice remains: prefer the official standard
properties, and keep custom ones to a minimum.

customProperties:
  - property: "legalEntity"
    value: "Insurance Corp AG"
    description: "Legal entity that owns and provides this data"

authoritativeDefinitions:
  - url: "https://example.com/apis/customers/openapi.yaml"
    type: "openapi"
    description: "OpenAPI specification of the REST API serving this data"

Data contracts rarely stand alone, and their value grows with what they
connect to. Three connections matter most in practice: link columns to
your domain model instead of restating their meaning, put contracts on the
ports of data products, and let the contract be the product page that
consumers request access from.

Especially when agents work with data and combine data from different
sources, documenting the semantics of individual datasets is not
enough. As pointed out in Making Your Data
Ready for Agentic AI, semantics need to be defined across data
sources in an overarching semantic layer. Combining semantics,
ontologies in particular, with data contracts solves two concrete
problems:

Metadata de-duplication: They reduce duplication for the data producer.
A concept such as Customer ID can be defined once, including its examples,
confidentiality and privacy classification, and description, and the data
contracts simply link to that definition, inheriting the centrally defined
characteristics rather than restating them.

Semantic consistency and interoperability: They make data from two or
more data contracts interoperable for the data consumer. By linking columns to a
shared conceptual definition, a consumer can tell whether two similarly named
columns actually mean the same thing, and whether two differently named ones do.
This is consistency at the conceptual level, not merely a matter of matching
primary and foreign keys, even though such a shared concept is exactly what
makes a reliable join key.
Figure 2: Two data contracts link their properties to the same concept in an ontology, so a consumer knows how to join them

schema:
  - name: "customer_360"
    properties:
      - name: "cid"
        authoritativeDefinitions:
          - type: "semantics"
            url: "https://example.com/ns/Customer.id"

The core concept is to point from the data contract to an element in
an ontology via an authoritativeDefinitions element. That way, the data
contract maps into the ontology. The element simply needs to be
identified by an IRI or URL within that ontology. The ontology itself
can be described using standards like RDF, OWL, or using the promising
ontology standard within the Apache Ossie
project, currently incubating at the Apache Software Foundation.
Data Products Build Upon Data Contracts

Data contracts go particularly well together with data
products, which bring product thinking to data, and are a central
part of modern, decentralized data architectures such as data
mesh. Data contracts are the interface description language that
makes the ports of a data product explicit and verifiable.
Figure 3: A data product with one input port and three output ports, each described by a data contract; two output ports offer different versions of the same contract

Since 2025, the family of Bitol standards also has a standard for
describing the metadata for data products, the Open Data Product
Standard (ODPS), building upon the Open Data Contract
Standard.
customers.odps.yaml, describing the Customers data product

apiVersion: "v1.1.0"
  kind: "DataProduct"
  id: "customers"
  name: "Customers"
  status: "active"
  
  description:
    purpose: >
      Master data for all customers holding a life insurance
      policy. All customers since 2020-01-01.
    usage: "Used by analytics teams for customer insights and cross-sell prediction"
    limitations: "Contains only customers with an active policy"
  
  inputPorts:
    - name: "customer_events"
      version: "1.0.0"
      contractId: "kafka_customer_events"
  
  outputPorts:
    - name: "customers_pii_snowflake_v1"
      description: "All customer records, with PII."
      version: "1.0.0"
      contractId: "customers_pii_snowflake"
    - name: "customers_pii_snowflake_v2"
      description: "All customer records, with PII."
      version: "2.0.0"
      contractId: "customers_pii_snowflake"
    - name: "customers_npii_snowflake_v1"
      description: "All customer records, without PII data."
      version: "1.0.0"
      contractId: "customers_npii_snowflake"

In the ODPS example above, the ports of a data product refer to
data contracts defined using ODCS. Together, the ODPS and ODCS files
form the data product metadata. The data product is the whole thing:
the code and the pipeline that produces the data, the data itself, and
the metadata that describes it. This is the concept of a data product
as an architectural quantum, a
self-contained unit with input and output ports as ODCS-specified
interfaces.

As the two standards are compatible with each other, we can move
the information regarding ownership, such as teams and support
channels, as well as information that applies to all data contracts,
into the data product description, reducing duplication.

As useful as data products and ODPS are, the data contracts at
the output ports remain the central element. They hold the promises
the provider makes, and many parties work with them.
Figure 4: The data contract is central to at least four parties: provider, consumer, data governance, and data product platform

The provider publishes the data contract, and consumers rely on
it. The data product platform reads it to know what to register,
provision, and monitor. Data governance reads it to check that
policies on ownership, classification, and terms of use are
followed. And that is why, in the end, the data contract is also
the product details page in a data marketplace.
Data Contracts are the “Product Details Page” in a Data Marketplace

Most enterprises have some sort of data marketplace, where data
becomes shoppable. There, data contracts contain all the information
for data consumers to make an informed decision about whether the
provided data is what they need for their intended purpose. When
convinced, a consumer requests access to the data described by the
contract, including a processing purpose that should be in line with
the terms of use of the data contract. This request is the
counterpart of a customer clicking “buy” on a product details
page.

The request creates an access agreement consisting
mainly of three parts: the requested data's data contract, the
stated processing purpose, and the requesting consumer. The access
agreement only becomes effective when the provider approves the
request. Only then does the data
product platform grant the actual data access.
Figure 5: An access agreement between the provider and an AI agent: the agent requests access, the provider approves, and the agent gets short-lived access to the data

Don't confuse the two. A data contract is published one-sidedly
by the provider, refers to no specific consumer, and has no notion
of time. An access agreement is bilateral, much closer to a contract
in everyday life: the consumer creates it as a request, and it only
becomes binding once the provider approves it, just as a contract
binds only when both parties have signed. It always has a start date
and, optionally, an expiration date; for AI agents, the granted
access period can be as short as a few minutes. There is no standard
for access agreements yet, but the Bitol project is working on one:
an RFC for an Open Access Agreement Standard (OAAS) proposes
recording who may access which output port, for what purpose, and
for how long.

A product page also shows reviews, not just the manufacturer's
description. The equivalent for data is the contract's track
record: with test results published to the marketplace, it can
show next to each promise how well it was kept, for example that
freshness was met on 29 of the last 30 days, or how long the team
typically takes to fix a broken promise. Such trust signals, as
described in Building an
“Amazon.com” for Your Data Products, tell a consumer more
than the promise alone.

Writing a data contract is the easy part; living with it is where
teams succeed or fail. Doing it well means treating a data contract with the same rigor as an
API: creating it deliberately, keeping it next to the code,
evolving it without breaking consumers, and checking it
automatically.

If data is already shared with other teams, for example as tables
in a data warehouse, we can put it under contract to make the promises
of the data provider explicit, ideally as the output port of a data
product. For that, we need to represent the existing structure of the
dataset in the data contract, and then add all the implicit promises
iteratively. This can be kickstarted by using the open source tool
Data Contract CLI that can convert existing metadata describing the
structure of the data such as SQL DDL, JSON Schema, or Avro Schema,
and generate a first draft of a data contract, which is enriched
afterwards.

Generation is only the starting point, though. Once the first
draft has been enriched and published, the direction flips: the
data contract is stable and becomes the source of truth, and the
data has to follow it. If a column in the underlying table is
renamed later, the contract is not regenerated. The contract test
fails instead, and the rename has to be handled as what it is: a
breaking change.

Another approach is to first start with a conversation on what
should actually be built, leading to defining the data contract before
any code is written. In our experience, a workshop format with a
facilitator works very well, where the potential provider of the data
and data consumers work together on a first draft of the data
contract.
You can capture this draft in whatever medium suits the group:
A whiteboard, or a YAML editor of your choice

The Data Product Canvas, in
which the data contract is a central part

An ODCS-compliant Excel template, the
tool that business users work with every day

The open source Data Contract
Editor

In the end, a standard-compliant data contract must emerge, which
is refined iteratively until all parties are satisfied, and then used
to start implementing the pipeline to actually provide the data
according to the agreed data contract.
Its Natural Habitat is a Git Repository

But regardless of how the data contract is created, its natural
habitat is the Git repository alongside its data product metadata,
the code that helps to produce the actual data, and the
configuration of the CI/CD pipeline. The contracts typically are
stored in a dedicated subfolder with the data product YAML being at
the root of the repository.
File tree of the Git repository of the Customers data product

customers.odps.yaml
  |- datacontracts
     |- customers_pii_snowflake_v1.odcs.yaml
     |- customers_pii_snowflake_v2.odcs.yaml
     |- customers_npii_snowflake_v1.odcs.yaml
  |- code
     |- pipeline.sql
  .gitlab-ci.yml

Our advice is to not place them far away from the pipeline code,
as the code for the pipeline typically has to change together with
the data contract. And things that change together should be put
together.

You might have noticed the naming convention for the filename
already. It starts with the human-readable ID of the data contract,
which names the dataset (customers_pii or customers_npii) and the
technology (snowflake) where the data is available for the consumer,
followed by the major version (v1 or v2). The major version is
part of the filename, but not of the ID: the ID stays the same
across major versions, so they can live side by side as separate
files. This is best practice as a data product can offer its
data in different forms, versions, and on different technologies.
Different environments such as test, staging, and production, are
best encoded within the data contract through separate server
entries.
The Story of Versioning and Breaking Changes

One of the main goals of data contracts is to find breaking
changes before consumers are affected, and offer graceful
evolution processes. For that, data contracts follow the
SemVer versioning scheme.

Major Version Change: Breaking change such as removing a column or renaming
it
Minor Version Change: Non-breaking change such as adding a new column

Patch Version Change: Small change such as fixing a typo or updating the
support channels

Breaking changes increase the major version, whereas non-breaking
changes or small fixes increase the minor or patch version. The
major version is tied to the dataset it protects. In case of a
major, breaking change, the data contract should be provided in an
incremented major version alongside a new dataset. This allows
phasing in a new major version next to an existing one, and after
some grace period, phasing out the old major version. During that
grace period, the status signals to the consumer whether it is being
phased in, active, or being phased out. The data contract typically
begins its life in the draft status, phasing in as being in
development, and marked as active if the promises are now actually
binding. The same holds for phasing it out, marking it as deprecated
and then retired. The lifecycle is heavily intertwined with the
versioning. When contracts are managed as part of a data product,
this lifecycle often follows the data product's release process
instead, with each major version offered as its own output port
running in parallel.

For event streams, this maps onto the compatibility modes of a
schema registry. A minor version has to be forward compatible, so
existing consumers keep reading new events with the schema they
already have, and ideally fully compatible, so new consumers can
also replay old events. Beware of the registry default: backward
compatibility permits deleting a field, which is exactly the change
that breaks existing consumers. Anything the registry would reject
is a major version, published as a new topic.

A data contract that nobody checks is a paper tiger: its promises
are worth no more than a wiki page, and the first time a consumer
finds one broken, their trust is gone. The real value comes with
automation on top of it, and the potential is huge:

Generate HTML documentation and make it centrally available in your
intranet

Publish to metadata repositories such as data product marketplaces or data
catalogs

Test the data in your test environment against the contract within your
CI/CD pipeline in your pull request and prevent a merge in case of failure

Test the data in your production environment against the contract every day
and inform the owner and any consumer downstream in case of broken promises

Generate the SQL DDL to create the tables from the data contract, making the
tables contract-compliant by design as the data provider

Derive masking and access policies on the data platform from the contract,
for example masking every column tagged pii:true for roles without
access to personal data

Generate the SQL query to actually use the data as a tolerant data consumer
without the select star operator

Compare the new version of a data contract with its old one in a pull
request and fail if there is a breaking change for only a minor or patch
version update

Validate new data against the contract before it reaches consumers, and hold

The open source tool Data Contract CLI, with over

understands data contracts in the ODCS format, and is useful to

Data Contracts Belong in Your CI/CD Pipeline

Data contracts belong in your CI/CD pipeline, where every commit
is checked before it ships. The Data Contract CLI offers a
command for each stage: datacontract lint validates the
contract, datacontract breaking catches breaking changes against
the previous version, and datacontract ci tests the data against the
contract in each environment. Only when all stages pass does the
pipeline deploy to production and publish the contract to the
marketplace with datacontract publish.

The Costs and Benefits of Data Contracts

Data contracts pay back in trust and automation, but they are not
free, and they are not worth writing for every dataset. Agents amplify
both sides of this trade-off.

When a large part of an enterprise's analytical data is described
by data contracts, the data can be tested automatically against the
promises in the contract. Its quality can be monitored continuously,
and when it falls below a promised threshold, counter-actions can be
triggered automatically.

At least as important, because consumers' expectations are written
down, changes that break them can be detected automatically, for
instance to stop a deployment in a CI/CD pipeline. Breaking changes no
longer propagate through pipelines into downstream services, which
makes the whole system far more robust.

Overall, data contracts shift ownership towards data providers.
That builds trust between providers and consumers, between business
and IT, and, increasingly, between humans and the agents working on
their behalf.

Each of these benefits grows when the consumer is an agent, because
an agent reads the contract literally and acts on it at machine speed.
A contract tells an agent what it needs to act safely and correctly:
the schema to query the data right, the semantics to combine it with
other datasets, the quality guarantees to trust it, and the terms of
use to know what it is allowed to do.

Two capabilities only become practical this way: generating your
data pipeline, and chatting with your data.

Data contracts enable spec-driven development. The data
contract acts as the core of the specification: fed into a coding
agent, alongside a plugin containing skills that describe how data
pipelines are built in your company, the agent can generate almost the
entire data pipeline automatically. An example run of such a
generation is available on dataproduct.com. During the generation of the
data pipeline, the data can be tested against the contract, acting as
a feedback loop, steering the agent in the right direction.
Figure 7: A coding agent generates the data pipeline from the data contract, skills, and the data marketplace

Business users want to ask questions like “Why is our revenue up
this quarter?” and get an answer within minutes. With “chat with your
data”, the hard part isn't generating SQL, it is generating the
correct SQL. Point your agent at the database with its hundreds of
tables and thousands of columns, and it has to guess the semantics of
the columns, and how to join the tables together correctly. And we
haven't even talked about whether it is allowed to answer the question
with this data.

But before an agent can query data correctly, it has to find it.
Published to a data marketplace that agents can search, for example
through MCP, data contracts make data discoverable in the first place.
Once found, a data contract stops the guessing. It tells the agent the
meaning of the columns, and through the semantic links that form the
context layer, how to join datasets correctly. Its terms of use make
it clear what is allowed to be done with the data, and what usages are
not. With that, “chat with your data” becomes something you can rely
on.

None of this comes for free. Data contracts take time and effort to
write and maintain, and their owners have to keep the promises in
them. Agents raise the stakes here too: an agent acts on an outdated
contract just as confidently as on a correct one.

That's why you should not introduce data contracts for all the data
in your company. It may sound like generic consultant advice, but it
matters: focus on the interfaces where one team shares data with
another, ideally via data products.

Also, don't roll out data contracts all at once. That feels like
bureaucracy if a contract does not immediately solve an actual
problem. Start where it hurts: data quality issues, broken pipelines,
or a lot of miscommunication. Or, when a new use case is being built,
specify its interfaces with data contracts right from the start.

Moreover, introducing data contracts is a cultural change towards
ownership of data, with explicit and verifiable promises. The standard
and tooling help, but teams have to learn that ownership also means
being responsible when something breaks. Making things explicit can
also reveal missing ownership, which then has to be fixed in the
organization first.

Providers are usually measured on shipping features, so a contract
can feel like friction with little payoff. A few things help: platform
templates that make writing and testing a contract cheap, workshops
with consumers to agree on the service levels they actually need,
showing each data product's reliability in the marketplace so that
good ownership gets noticed, and making clear who owns the alert when
a promise breaks.

The cost is real, but data contracts offer a high payoff through
establishing trust, making automation possible, and empowering agents.
When introduced with care, they pay off sooner rather than later.
Why Data Contracts Will Be Everywhere

With ODCS, data contracts have a de facto industry standard,
governed at the Linux Foundation, and open source tooling around it.
We believe that soon data contracts will be for data what OpenAPI is
for REST APIs today, for three reasons: agents finally make it
worthwhile to write them well, consumers will start writing their own,
and an open standard keeps them portable.
In the Age of Agents, the Incentive Points the Right Way

Data contracts are valuable even without AI agents. But the
effort goes into the parts that can be automated. Schema and quality
rules are filled out with care; the prose fields such as business
names, descriptions, and terms of use are not filled out with the
same rigor, as they are only read by other humans. Sad, but
true.

Agents change that. An agent takes those prose fields at their
word and acts on them. A vague description leads it to build the
wrong pipeline, a missing “terms of use” leads it to use the data in
ways it shouldn't, and an ambiguous purpose leads to a confidently
wrong answer. Suddenly, the neglected half of the contract has real
consequences, and the incentive finally points the right way. The
standard is already following: ODCS 3.2 added the AI context, a
block written for agents.

Metadata used to be a chore done for other people, so it
languished at the bottom of the backlog. Now it pays you back: ask a
question, see a wrong answer, fix the description or the terms of
use, ask again. Few people write documentation for someone else's
benefit, but when the benefit is their own, the metadata gets
better. This is the forcing function: agents finally make it
worthwhile to write the whole contract well, which is exactly why,
in the age of agents, data contracts will flourish.
Consumer-Driven Data Contracts Add the Missing Perspective

So far, we have looked at data contracts published by providers
so that consumers can trust the data. But trust also has to run the
other way, for example when sharing sensitive data, which is what
the terms of use are for.

Applying the principle of consumer-driven
contracts to data contracts
goes one step further: a consumer can publish their own data contract,
specifying their promises and expectations in the same structured
way that we looked at the provider side so far. In fact, we can use
the exact same ODCS-defined structure to describe a consumer-driven
contract, because it is just the direction that changes: whereas for
instance a schema-definition in the provider-driven contract states
a promise, in the consumer-driven contract, it states an
expectation.

This also allows contract-first from the consumer side: a
consumer specifies the data they need without knowing who could
provide it, and the specification is used to find matching data,
which becomes especially powerful when an AI agent does the search.
Consumer-driven contracts also document which data is actually used
compared to what access was granted, which helps providers optimize
their service and automate governance.

Metadata is tiny in volume but strategically central: it is the
map to all your valuable data and the foundation every catalog,
quality check, lineage tool, and AI agent builds upon. That is
exactly why large vendors are happy to give their metadata solution
away for free. It is not out of generosity, but because once your
metadata lives in their proprietary format, everything reading it is
locked in too. Since metadata is so small, there is no storage or
cost reason to keep it proprietary. Doing so is purely a play for
control.

An open standard is the only real defense. It keeps your metadata
portable, lets you combine best-of-breed tools from different
vendors, and puts the format under vendor-neutral governance. ODCS
lives at the Linux Foundation, so no single company can change the
rules. Pioneering companies had to build custom formats and tooling
from scratch, while recent adopters build on ODCS and its open
ecosystem at a fraction of the effort. A simple test of whether you
are locked in: can you export all your contracts as plain files into
git and rebuild your catalog elsewhere from them alone? And as
agents become the primary consumers of metadata, whoever controls
its format controls access to your enterprise data. OpenAPI has
already shown the alternative for operational systems: it is itself
an open metadata standard, describing REST APIs in a vendor-neutral
format that any gateway, generator, or documentation tool can read.
ODCS brings the same to data. Those who embrace open
standards keep sovereignty over their metadata.
